tldr: On a bipedal robot mounted with a single robotic arm, a whole-body control policy trained with reinforcement learning autonomously coordinates arm reaching, postural adaptations like squatting, and stepping purely from 6-DoF end-effector targets, requiring no base-velocity or footstep commands.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed system. Taking a 6-DoF end-effector target pose and state history as inputs, it directly controls all 14 joints of the whole body using a temporal context estimator combining a Transformer and GRU along with reward gating, executing diverse high-level commands such as VR teleoperation and diffusion policies.
overview:
For a robot to manipulate objects located beyond the arm's reach, loco-manipulation—coordinating leg and torso motions with arm movements to crouch or walk closer—is essential. However, bipedal robots always carry the risk of falling, requiring them to simultaneously satisfy conflicting demands: end-effector positioning accuracy, locomotive propulsion, and dynamic balance maintenance. Prior research typically separated the locomotion and manipulation controllers or explicitly commanded base movement velocities and foot placement locations from higher-level planners.

In response, this study focuses on an extremely simple common interface: providing only a 6-DoF target pose for the end-effector. The policy is designed to handle whole-body coordinated motions entirely within a single model—reaching with the arm if the target is close, squatting if it is low, and taking a step forward if it is far away. To achieve this, the authors devised a biped-specific reward gating strategy that switches safety metrics between locomotion and precise manipulation phases, as well as a temporal context estimator combining a Transformer and GRU to infer unobserved dynamics from observation history.

The policy was trained via large-scale parallel reinforcement learning in a physics simulator (Isaac Lab) and zero-shot transferred to a low-cost real robot (LimX TRON 1 + ARX L5). Experiments demonstrated that the exact same policy could directly execute three entirely different types of high-level commands: VR teleoperation, an imitation-learned diffusion policy, and scripted trajectories. Furthermore, compared to conventional floating-base inverse kinematics (IK) control, the vertical workspace expanded significantly, enabling stable tracking without oscillation even in extreme postures such as deep squats and high reaches.
contributions: Formulating and realizing bipedal whole-body control that autonomously coordinates reaching, postural adaptation, and stepping from only a single 6-DoF end-effector target pose, requiring no base-velocity, step-length, or gait commands.

Introducing phase-aware reward gating that switches conflicting safety criteria between locomotion and manipulation, alongside a best-so-far progress reward, reconciling end-effector tracking with fall prevention.
Proposing a temporal context estimator that combines a Transformer to capture local short-term dependencies with a GRU to retain long-term memory, trained via an auxiliary dynamics prediction task.

Deploying on a low-cost physical bipedal mobile manipulator to serve as a shared execution layer across different high-level commands (VR teleoperation, diffusion policy, scripted trajectories), and demonstrating vertical workspace expansion beyond floating-base IK.

sections.heading: Can a bipedal robot walk, crouch, and reach given only an end-effector target?
sections.summary: This section discusses the significance and challenges of integrated locomotion and manipulation control for bipedal robots to interact beyond arm workspace limits. It proposes a framework where high-level commands are restricted purely to 6-DoF end-effector targets, letting the controller autonomously decide base movement and gait patterns.
sections.details:
Fixed-base arms have a physical limit to their reachable workspace. Overcoming this requires loco-manipulation, which coordinates leg locomotion with arm manipulation. This study adopts a minimal 14-DoF robot setup consisting of a bipedal leg base mounted with a single 6-axis robotic arm. Compared to full-body humanoids, it offers a more practical, low-cost hardware configuration, yet it requires coordinating end-effector reaching, postural adaptations like lowering the hips, and stepping without disrupting the biped's fragile balance.

A key design philosophy here is restricting the task command to the controller solely to the end-effector's 6-DoF pose (position and orientation). If a high-level layer has to specify instructions like moving the base at a certain speed or stepping the left foot forward, task design becomes tightly bound to the whole body's complex geometry and dynamics. By decoupling via a geometrically clean interface like end-effector poses, the same low-level controller can be reused seamlessly whether driven by human teleoperation or learned manipulation policies.

However, this formulation faces two difficult challenges. The first is reconciling competing demands among end-effector tracking, locomotion, and balance maintenance. Adopting an unnatural posture to zero out end-effector error can lead to a fall. The second is that unobserved dynamics—such as contact states, disturbances, and hardware characteristics—must be inferred and adapted to from limited on-board sensor histories. This study resolves both challenges simultaneously through reinforcement learning combining reward gating with a Transformer–GRU temporal estimator.

captions.F1: System overview of the proposed method. During training, it uses reward gating and a critic with privileged information, while the temporal estimator summarizes history with a Transformer and GRU. During deployment, it outputs whole-body joint position commands using only the end-effector target pose and sensor readings, supporting diverse high-level inputs.

sections.heading: Prior work in quadrupeds and humanoids, and the unique position of this work
sections.summary: Prior research on learning-based loco-manipulation and task-space interfaces is reviewed. While quadruped bases and dual-arm humanoids are predominant, this study takes a unique approach by coordinating all 14 whole-body joints end-to-end on a minimal bipedal, single-arm platform.
sections.details:
### II-A RL-Based Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
Reinforcement learning for whole-body coordinated control first achieved major milestones in quadrupedal robot manipulation. Prior works coordinated arms with four legs to expand reaching ranges or directly integrated visual feedback. For humanoids, approaches have emerged such as learning a single whole-body tracking policy (ULC), adopting hierarchical structures where upper-body motions counteract walking sway (SEEC), or decoupling world-frame planning from low-level execution (HiWET).
In contrast, this study focuses on a minimal hardware setup: a bipedal base with a single arm. Rather than separating upper- and lower-body controllers, a single policy directly commands all 14 joints across the whole body, autonomously eliciting postural adaptations and stepping motions under the strict dynamic balance constraints of a biped.

### II-B Task-Space Interfaces for Loco-Manipulation
How high-level task commands are decoupled from low-level whole-body control is crucial to overall versatility. Many prior studies handled base walking with a separate policy while tracking end-effector poses, or combined base (root) or torso targets alongside end-effector trajectories. While works like RFM (Reward Fusion Module) drive the whole body solely from 6-DoF end-effector targets on wheeled quadrupeds, this study extends that concept to the unstable dynamics of bipedal walking. By eliminating any specification of base velocity or gait phase, it achieves a pure task-space interface that accepts only instantaneous 6-DoF end-effector targets.

sections.heading: Architecture and reward design: Tracking the end-effector while preventing biped falls
sections.summary: This section details the overall control pipeline, the temporal context estimator fusing a Transformer and GRU, and the biped-specific reward gating strategy. Unobserved dynamic properties are extracted as latent variables from state history, smoothly switching competing safety criteria between locomotion and stationary manipulation.
sections.details:
### III-A Training Pipeline and Control Loop
The overall control setup is straightforward. At each control step, a 9-dimensional command $\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{ee}}_{t}$ is provided, consisting of the target end-effector position and a 6D continuous rotation matrix representation defined in the base frame. The 58-dimensional observation $\mathbf{o}_t$ includes base angular velocity, gravity vector, joint positions and velocities, end-effector pose, and the previous action. Crucially, base linear velocity and foot contact parameters are excluded from policy inputs and fed only to the Critic in an Asymmetric Actor-Critic framework. The 14-dimensional normalized action $\mathbf{a}_t$ produced by the Actor represents target joint displacements for the 8 leg joints (scaled by 0.6), the 3 shoulder/arm-base joints (0.3), and the 3 wrist joints (0.2), which are tracked by a low-level PD controller running at 500 Hz.

### III-B Temporal Context Estimation with Transformer + GRU
To handle unknown payload variations, floor friction, and external disturbances, dynamic context is inferred from the past 10 steps ($H=10$) of proprioceptive history $\mathbf{H}_t$. First, a Transformer's self-attention mechanism extracts local dynamic responses within the 10-step window, and its output is passed to a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) to maintain long-term context spanning beyond those 10 steps. From this representation, the network estimates base linear velocity $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t$ and parameterizes the mean and variance of a latent distribution to sample a latent vector. During training, an MLP decoder is tasked with predicting the next observation vector $\mathbf{y}_{t+1}$ as an auxiliary task, trained alongside KL regularization ($\beta=0.1$). This auxiliary loss allows the policy to capture the latent representation $\mathbf{z}_t$ needed for dynamics adaptation without directly observing physical environmental parameters.

### III-C Biped-Aware Reward Gating
A phase variable $g_t$ transitions based on the remaining distance to the target, shifting emphasis toward locomotion and whole-body approach when far, and toward high-precision tracking and stabilization when near. The core of this method lies in defining distinct safety scores for the locomotion phase ($s_t^l$) and manipulation phase ($s_t^m$). During locomotion, where legs must move substantially, foot placement and base orientation are monitored; during stationary manipulation, base and joint velocity residuals are strictly checked to suppress wobble. To prevent the task learning signal from vanishing entirely when the safety score drops near zero due to transient disturbances, a bounded gate $\tilde{s}_t^q$ cushioned with a lower bound offset $c_s$ multiplies the task reward. Furthermore, the progress reward adopts a Best-so-far Progress formulation that only rewards improvements over the minimum error achieved so far within the episode, curbing unnecessary oscillating motions.

sections.heading: Rigorous simulation benchmarks and versatile real-robot demonstrations
sections.summary: Ablation experiments in Isaac Lab confirmed that the proposed reward gating and temporal context estimator contribute significantly to success rate and motion smoothness. Physical robot experiments showed that the same controller executed VR teleoperation, a diffusion policy, and trajectory tracking, while vastly outperforming floating-base IK in vertical workspace.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The physical platform consists of a LimX TRON 1 bipedal base, an ARX L5 6-axis arm, a GENROBOT UMI gripper, a Livox Mid-360 LiDAR, and an on-board NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX for computation. Robot pose is estimated via FAST-LIO2 LiDAR-inertial odometry, combined with forward kinematics to compute the current end-effector pose. Reinforcement learning was conducted in Isaac Lab across 8,192 parallel environments for 20,000 iterations (approx. 28 hours on an RTX 5090). The policy operates at 50 Hz, and joint PD control runs at 500 Hz.

### IV-B Simulation Evaluation and Ablations
Evaluations were conducted across 3 random seeds with 1,000 episodes each (success defined as position error < 5 cm and orientation error < 7 deg during the final 1 second).
- Reward Gating Comparison: Compared to an additive baseline, the success rate improved from 82.73% to 88.30%, and the 95th percentile (P95) position error dropped substantially from 14.35 cm to 5.38 cm. Action variation also decreased from 0.218 to 0.165, yielding noticeably smoother motions.
- Temporal Context Estimator Comparison: Without latent variables (No-latent), the success rate fell to 69.87%. Transformer-only reached 84.43% and GRU-only reached 82.23%, whereas the proposed hybrid method attained 88.30%. This is close to the privileged oracle (94.53%), proving that the observation history effectively recovers necessary dynamics information.

### IV-C Real-Robot Deployment and Workspace Verification
On the physical robot, the exact same trained policy executed three distinct high-level inputs without any controller modifications:
- VR Teleoperation: Driven by a human operator using a Meta Quest headset, the robot crouched to grasp a plush toy on the floor, took steps forward to place it on a shelf, and picked up an eraser to wipe a whiteboard continuously.
- Diffusion Policy: Receiving end-effector targets from a policy trained on UMI-style demonstration data, the robot autonomously pushed a cabinet door shut.
- Scripted Trajectories: Tracking periodic vertical end-effector motions to evaluate height adaptation.
Compared to conventional floating-base IK control, the vertical workspace expanded dramatically from 38–163 cm with IK to 3–191 cm with the proposed method. The robot demonstrated robust tracking without foot vibration even in extreme postures, spanning deep floor-level squats to tall standing stretches.

captions.F2: Appearance of the physical robot platform. Equipped with an ARX L5 arm, UMI gripper, Livox LiDAR, and Jetson Orin NX on a LimX TRON 1 bipedal base, running all state estimation and inference fully on-board.
captions.F6: Comparison of vertical workspace on the real robot. While conventional floating-base + IK (cyan) is limited to 38–163 cm, the proposed method (red) autonomously coordinates deep squatting and stretching, expanding the reach to 3–191 cm.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future outlook: Toward more dynamic and precise loco-manipulation
sections.summary: This section concludes the learned bipedal manipulator controller that achieves whole-body coordination solely from end-effector target poses. Future directions include extending to more dynamic loco-manipulation and improving end-effector accuracy for fine manipulation tasks.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated a bipedal whole-body controller trained via reinforcement learning that autonomously links arm reaching, postural adaptations like squatting, and stepping purely from a single 6-DoF end-effector target pose. Key innovations include phase-aware reward gating that resolves conflicts between bipedal locomotion and end-effector tracking, and a Transformer–GRU temporal estimator that captures both short- and long-term observation dependencies.

Simulations and hardware trials proved that a single policy serves as a unified execution foundation across disparate inputs: human VR teleoperation, a pre-trained diffusion policy, and scripted trajectories. In addition, it achieved a substantially broader workspace and superior dynamic stability compared to geometric IK-based control.

Looking ahead, the authors highlight expanding to agile, highly dynamic motions and enhancing tracking precision for delicate tasks such as fine assembly—especially when following noisy commands from learned high-level policies—as key directions for future research.

takeaways: Using only a 6-DoF end-effector target pose as the unified low-level interface cleanly decouples high-level planners (VR, imitation learning, trajectory generators) from whole-body motion generation.

Because bipedal loco-manipulation imposes distinct safety requirements across locomotion and manipulation phases, phase-dependent reward gating with a lower-bound cushion (preventing zeroed gates) is vital for training stability.

Fusing short-term self-attention (Transformer) with long-term recurrence (GRU) alongside an auxiliary next-state prediction task allows unobserved system dynamics to be accurately captured into a latent representation from on-board proprioception.

Reinforcement-learning-based whole-body coordination suppresses vibrations near workspace boundaries (extreme low and high reaches) compared to geometric IK solvers, substantially expanding the usable operational envelope.
limitations: For precision manipulation requiring fine positioning, end-effector tracking accuracy leaves room for improvement, particularly when tracking noisy commands from learned high-level policies like diffusion policies.
Current behaviors primarily focus on quasi-static reaches and gentle stepping; scaling to highly dynamic whole-body loco-manipulation involving running or jumping remains future work.

Evaluated environmental variations were mainly limited to flat-ground friction changes, payload shifts, and modest external pushes, leaving whole-body coordination on uneven terrain or stair environments unassessed.
